snippet.title: Carlo Rovelli: Are we sleepwalking towards nuclear war?
snippet.description:
We're closer to nuclear catastrophe than at any point since the Cold War. That's the warning from theoretical physicist Carlo Rovelli.

Drawing on his new book “85 Seconds to Midnight”, Rovelli argues that fear, not strength, is driving a dangerous new global arms race. He explains why he believes humanity has forgotten the lessons of Hiroshima, why today's rearmament risks repeating the mistakes of history, and how artificial intelligence could make the threat of nuclear war even greater.

In this episode of Ways to Change the World, Krishnan Guru-Murthy speaks to theoretical physicist and bestselling author Carlo Rovelli about nuclear weapons, the morality of science, international cooperation and why he believes humanity's greatest enemy is its own irrationality.

The $80 Billion World Cup: Who Really Profits? - The World Cup is not just a football tournament. It is a global economic machine involving tourism, hotels, transportation, brands, media rights, public spending, security, visas, city branding and international power. This documentary explores who really profits from the World Cup — and who pays the price to make it happen.

The $80 Billion World Cup: Who Really Profits? (2026)

Synopsis:
As the World Cup returns to North America, the tournament promises billions of dollars in global spending and a historic opportunity for the United States, Mexico and Canada. But behind the celebration of football lies a much bigger economic story.

This documentary examines how the World Cup has become one of the most powerful business platforms in global sports. Host cities expect tourism, hotel bookings, restaurant spending and international visibility. Brands see a massive consumer market. Major League Soccer sees a chance to accelerate the growth of soccer in the United States. Investors see clubs, stadiums, media rights and players becoming long-term assets.

But the economic promise comes with a cost. Fans face expensive tickets, dynamic pricing, transportation costs and secondary market speculation. Cities must invest in security, transit, public spaces and Fan Fests. The United States must also prove it can handle the logistics, visas, immigration questions and diplomatic pressure of welcoming the world.

And beyond 2026, the race to host mega-events continues. Saudi Arabia’s 2034 World Cup bid shows how countries now use football as a tool for tourism, infrastructure, national branding and global influence.

The World Cup generates money. The real question is: who captures that value — and who pays the price to create it?

snippet.title: Life After Death : Should organ donation be mandatory? | Rayan Mian | TEDxDAA Youth
snippet.description: Rayan explores the urgent issue of organ donation and the lives lost while waiting for transplants. He examines the limitations of the current opt-in system and proposes making organ donation the default after death. Using examples from countries such as Spain and Austria, he shows how policy can increase donation rates and save more lives. He also addresses ethical and religious concerns. Ultimately, Rayan challenges audiences to rethink legacy, suggesting the greatest gift is the chance for others to live. Rayan Mian is a 10th grader from Pakistan who is deeply interested in the healthcare system and enjoys working on research-based projects that explore real-world issues. His curiosity about medicine and public health inspired him to investigate organ donation and the impact policy can have on saving lives. This talk was given at a TEDx event using the TED conference format but independently organized by a local community. Learn more at https://www.ted.com/tedx

When A Reporter Literally Ran Off Mid-Sentence for His Baby.

During a live ESPN segment, reporter Erin Hawksworth was discussing upcoming NFL Divisional Round matchups when something unexpected interrupted the broadcast. A sudden loud noise triggered confusion in the studio, forcing her to pause mid-sentence and quickly assess what was happening. Without hesitation, she apologized to her co-hosts and stepped away from the camera. It was later confirmed that a fire alarm had gone off in the building, prompting an immediate evacuation response. The moment highlights how unpredictable live television can be, where professional composure can shift instantly into real-world urgency. Even in a controlled studio environment, safety situations take priority over everything else, no matter how seamless the broadcast appears.

snippet.title: Psychology of People Who Think Too Much | Psychology explain
snippet.description:
People Who Think Too Much | Psychology explain

Do you find yourself replaying conversations from days ago? Do you struggle to stay present because your mind is constantly rehearsing the future or dissecting the past? In this video, we explore the deep psychological roots of overthinking and rumination. We dive into the 'Default Mode Network' of the brain, why intelligence often turns inward as a trap, and why your mind might actually feel safer in chaos than in calm. This isn't just about 'thinking less'—it's about understanding that your brain is trying to protect you in the only way it knows how. Learn how to create space between you and your thoughts and finally find a peace that doesn't require solving every problem.
